name: Taylor's Law
statement: Across sampled populations, the variance in a species' abundance grows as a power of its mean abundance.
statementAccent: grows as a power of its mean abundance
meaning: Taylor's law, or Taylor's power law, is an empirical regularity in ecology stating that the variance of the number or density of individuals of a species across a set of sampling areas is related to the corresponding mean by a power law: variance equals a constant times the mean raised to an exponent. On log-log axes this is a straight line whose slope is the exponent. The exponent measures how clumped the organisms are, and the law holds so broadly, across thousands of species and far beyond ecology, that it ranks among the most widely verified quantitative patterns in the life sciences, even as the mechanism behind it remains debated.
mechanism: Write the variance of abundance as a coefficient times the mean raised to an exponent, and take logarithms to get a straight line on log-log axes with the exponent as its slope. An exponent of one corresponds to a random, Poisson spatial distribution, in which variance equals the mean; an exponent above one signals aggregation, individuals clumped together, with values commonly between one and two and often near two. The exponent thus serves as a species-specific index of how strongly individuals cluster in space. Many mechanisms have been proposed to generate the pattern, from animal movement behaviour to birth-death-immigration processes, but none is agreed.

examples.text: L. R. Taylor found the variance-to-mean power law across many insect populations, the entomological data from which he first drew the law in 1961.
The same pattern appears in disease case counts, crime statistics, financial market data, gene expression, and even the distribution of prime numbers, showing its striking generality.
Pest managers use the fitted exponent to design sampling schemes, working out how many samples are needed to estimate a population's density to a target precision.

variants.name: Fluctuation scaling
variants.text: The same variance-versus-mean power law is known in physics as fluctuation scaling, of which Taylor's law is the ecological instance, a pattern seen across many complex systems.

variants.name: The aggregation index
variants.text: Taylor's proposal that the exponent be read as a species-specific measure of spatial clumping, from random at one to strongly aggregated as it rises toward two and beyond.

whyItMatters: Taylor's law is one of ecology's most robust empirical patterns, documented in over a thousand studies and across a startling range of systems, from insects and fish to epidemics, markets, and genomes. It gives a compact, practical description of how the variability of a population scales with its size, underpins the design of sampling and pest-management surveys, and connects ecology to the broader physics of fluctuation scaling. Its very generality raises a deep question, still unresolved, of whether it reflects real biology or is a near-inevitable statistical consequence of how means and variances relate.

working.text: expect the variance of a species' abundance to scale as a power of its mean, appearing as a straight line on log-log axes.
take an exponent of one as random spacing and values above one as aggregation, using it as an index of how clumped individuals are.
use the fitted exponent to plan how many samples are needed to estimate density to a chosen precision.

limits: Taylor's law is primarily an empirical pattern with a contested mechanism, and there is genuine debate over whether it reflects biological processes or is largely a statistical artefact of how means and variances relate, since the power-law variance function can arise from many families of distributions. It can fit poorly at low densities, where means are small, and estimated exponents are sensitive to the sampling scheme, spatial and temporal scale, and estimation method, so sample and population exponents can differ. The exponent is not a fixed universal constant but varies by species and context, most often between one and two though occasionally higher.
misreadings: The exponent is not a fixed universal constant; it varies by species, scale, and context. A straight line on log-log axes does not by itself prove an underlying biological mechanism, since the pattern can be a statistical consequence of the distribution's form. An exponent of one, not zero, marks the random, Poisson baseline, and it should not be confused with constant variance. And while the exponent usually lies between one and two, that is a common range rather than a strict ceiling, since higher values are sometimes reported.
origin: Formulated by the British entomologist and ecologist Lionel Roy Taylor in his 1961 paper 'Aggregation, variance and the mean' in Nature; the name Taylor's law was coined by Southwood in 1966.
